model.label: Mandatory, community-rated basic health insurance (OKP/LAMal) bought from competing private non-profit insurers, with income-tested premium subsidies from the cantons and federal government, and cantonal co-funding of hospital care

overview.statement: Since 1996, Swiss residents have been obliged to buy mandatory health insurance (MHI) from one of several competing insurers, and insurers must take every applicant whatever their individual risk.

The current system rests on the Federal Health Insurance Act (KVG) of 1994, in force since 1996, which brought near-universal compulsory coverage, a standard benefit package, community-rated premiums and income-based subsidies, and obliged insurers to accept all applicants.

locator.section: Coverage and Access: Background and History

overview.statement: Every resident must take out basic insurance (OKP) within three months of birth or of arriving in Switzerland; the obligation also covers undocumented migrants, and those who cannot pay depend on non-governmental organizations for care, according to the Commonwealth Fund profile.

locator.section: The Role of Public Health Insurance

overview.statement: According to the Commonwealth Fund profile, the whole population (100%) was covered by basic insurance (OKP) in 2023.

locator.section: The Role of Public Health Insurance

overview.statement: Although sold by private insurers, basic insurance (OKP) is tightly regulated, has a standard benefit package and is publicly subsidized, so the Commonwealth Fund treats it as Switzerland's public insurance model.

Health care responsibilities are split across federal, cantonal and municipal government; the cantons have wide autonomy over provision, financing, prevention and health promotion, though they increasingly work together.
Through direct democracy, voters can shape health policy by popular initiatives and referendums, for example on curbing health spending growth, presumed consent for organ donation and COVID-19 rules.

financing.statement: Basic insurance premiums are community-rated rather than tied to income; to help low-income households, the cantons pay premium subsidies.
Swiss health care cost CHF 97 billion in 2024, over 4% more than in 2023, according to the Federal Statistical Office.

By the Federal Statistical Office's count of who finances health care, households paid 21.3% of 2024 health costs directly out of pocket and 40.7% indirectly, mostly through health insurance premiums; most of the remaining 31.3% came from the public sector, chiefly the cantons.

locator.section: Die Haushalte tragen den Grossteil der Gesundheitskosten

financing.statement: Between 2023 and 2024, health spending by households rose 5.8% and by the state 5.7%, while companies' social insurance contributions to health fell 3.1% (Federal Statistical Office).

locator.section: Die Haushalte tragen den Grossteil der Gesundheitskosten

financing.statement: On WHO's definitions, public sources (mainly federal and cantonal tax revenue) funded only 36.2% of Swiss current health spending in 2021, against an EU average of 76.7%.

Mandatory insurance premiums, which WHO classes as compulsory prepayment rather than public spending, paid for another 34.5% of current health spending in 2021; public and premium funding together came to about 68.7%, below the EU average of 78.3%.
Public spending on health equalled 4.3% of GDP in 2021, well below the EU average of 7.1%.
Counting mandatory insurance premiums together with public spending, these financing schemes equalled 8.1% of GDP in 2021, above the EU average of 7.2%.

In 2023, total Swiss health costs were CHF 95 billion, of which about CHF 52 billion were services covered by basic insurance (OKP); about CHF 36 billion of those were paid for by insured people's premiums.
The share of total health costs paid by premiums rose from just under 30% when the KVG took effect in 1996 to just under 38% in 2023.
The average basic insurance premium for 2027 is CHF 412 a month, 5.0% (CHF 19.70) more than in 2026.
For 2027 the average monthly premium rises to CHF 487.60 for adults (+4.9%), CHF 338.80 for young adults (+4.8%) and CHF 128.10 for children (+4.6%).

The FOPH's average premium is all premiums paid in Switzerland divided by the number of insured; what a person actually pays depends on, among other things, where they live, their age, the deductible chosen, the insurer and the insurance model.
Premiums must cover the expected costs for each insurer in each canton, so rising basic insurance costs feed directly into higher premiums.

As a social counterweight to flat per-person premiums, the KVG requires cantons to reduce premiums for insured people of modest means, and for lower- and middle-income families to cut children's premiums by at least 80% and those of young adults in education by at least 50%.
Since 2008 the federal government has paid 7.5% of the gross costs of basic insurance towards premium reductions, shared among the cantons by resident population; the cantons add their own funds.
About CHF 6.6 billion in premium reductions were paid out in 2024, just over half of it (CHF 3.3 billion, 50.6%) from the federal government.

Under current rules the cantons pay at least 55% of the cost of inpatient hospital care and premiums at most 45%; outpatient care is paid entirely from premiums; and for nursing care basic insurance and patients each contribute, with the cantons covering the rest.

covered.statement: The basic benefit package is set by federal law and covers a broad range of services, including GP and specialist consultations, inpatient care and some services from other health professionals when a physician refers the patient.
Coverage gaps remain in the basic package, for example limited cover for dental care and vision aids.
Dental care is paid mostly out of pocket: in 2021, 78% of health spending on dental care came from out-of-pocket payments.

Psychotherapy is covered by basic insurance, but reimbursement often requires a medical prescription or referral, and the supply of therapists differs considerably by canton, region and language area.

By law, every covered service must be reviewed regularly against the criteria of effectiveness, appropriateness and cost-effectiveness (WZW); a service that no longer meets them is no longer reimbursed by basic insurance.

In the federal health technology assessment (HTA) programme, federal expert commissions appraise each HTA report and make a recommendation; the Federal Department of Home Affairs, or the FOPH for medicines, then decides whether to keep, restrict or remove coverage, and the decision is published.
The Federal Council has rejected moving services that meet the WZW criteria out of basic insurance into supplementary insurance, arguing that it would create two-tier medicine.

cost_sharing.statement: Adults choose an annual deductible within a legal range: the minimum is CHF 300, with optional higher levels of CHF 500, 1,000, 1,500, 2,000 or 2,500. Above the deductible patients pay 10% co-payment up to CHF 700 a year.
A higher deductible buys a lower premium, but the European Observatory notes these charges can deter or delay needed care, particularly for people on lower incomes or with chronic conditions.
Children under 18 do not pay the deductible; the 10% coinsurance on costs above the deductible is capped at CHF 700 a year for adults and CHF 350 for children.
A hospital contribution of CHF 15 per day applies with no time limit, with exemptions for children, young adults in education and maternity-related stays.
Women pay no deductible or coinsurance for prenatal, childbirth and postnatal care.

To steer patients to cheaper medicines, the co-payment on an originator or reference drug can be as high as 40% when a lower-cost generic or biosimilar exists; the measures are expected to save CHF 250 million a year, though there are worries about affordability for patients.
Out-of-pocket payments made up 23% of current health spending in 2021, above the EU average of 19%.
Between 2000 and 2021, out-of-pocket payments per person grew faster than GDP (3.1% against 1.1%), even though their share of spending fell for much of that period.

financial_hardship.statement: In 2022, the most common payment arrears in Switzerland were on taxes and on health insurance premiums: 5.5% and 4.4% of the population respectively lived in a household with such arrears (Federal Statistical Office, SILC survey).

locator.section: 5,5% de la population vit dans un ménage ayant au moins un arriéré d'impôt

financial_hardship.statement: In the Federal Statistical Office's survey, arrears are bills that could not be paid on time for financial reasons; health insurance premiums are one of the categories counted, alongside rent, utilities, credit repayments, taxes and others.

locator.section: 5,5% de la population vit dans un ménage ayant au moins un arriéré d'impôt

financial_hardship.statement: When an insured person does not pay premiums or cost-sharing, the insurer sends a reminder, then a demand for payment, and finally starts debt enforcement proceedings.
If enforcement ends in a certificate of unpaid debt (Verlustschein), the canton pays the insurer 85% of the outstanding claims.

locator.section: Übernahme der ausstehenden Prämien und Kostenbeteiligungen durch die Kantone

financial_hardship.statement: Cantons may put people who still do not pay their premiums after enforcement on a list; insurers then suspend paying for their care, except emergency treatment, until the debt is settled.

locator.section: Kantonale Liste der Versicherten, die ihre Prämien nicht zahlen

additional_care.statement: Voluntary health insurance can top up basic cover, for example for a semi-private or private hospital ward or dental care; its premiums are usually risk-rated and it is sold by for-profit companies.

According to the Commonwealth Fund profile, 28% of people voluntarily buy supplementary private insurance, which covers things outside basic insurance such as dental care, alternative medicine, private or semi-private hospital rooms and care abroad.

locator.section: The Role of Private Health Insurance

additional_care.statement: Supplementary insurance is not bound by the rules for universal access: insurers can turn applicants down and set premiums by health status, age and sex.

locator.section: The Role of Private Health Insurance

additional_care.statement: Voluntary health insurance paid for 6.6% of current health spending in 2021, much more than the EU average of 3.7%.

access.statement: Patients can generally choose their doctors and hospitals and see them without a referral.

locator.section: 3 Generating resources, providing services and ensuring access

access.statement: In 2021, 76% of insured people were in alternative insurance plans that restrict their choice of provider, such as HMO models.

locator.section: 3 Generating resources, providing services and ensuring access

access.statement: The standard basic plan allows direct access to specialists, but about 70% of people choose cheaper plans that require seeing a primary care provider first.
Switzerland had 444 physicians per 100,000 people in 2021, above the averages for the WHO European Region (389) and the EU (412).

locator.section: 3 Generating resources, providing services and ensuring access

access.statement: Nurse density, at 1,842 per 100,000 people in 2021, is among the highest in the WHO European Region, far above the regional (803) and EU (838) averages.

locator.section: 3 Generating resources, providing services and ensuring access

access.statement: The nurse figures are high partly because they count nursing-related staff trained at secondary level, who do not have the competencies or scope of practice of tertiary-trained nurses.

locator.section: 3 Generating resources, providing services and ensuring access

access.statement: Switzerland had 444 hospital beds per 100,000 people in 2021, below the WHO European Region average of 470 and nearly a third fewer than the 629 of 2000.

locator.section: 3 Generating resources, providing services and ensuring access

outcomes.statement: Life expectancy at birth was 83.7 years in 2022, far above the WHO European Region average (78.2) and higher than in France (82.3), Italy (82.8) and Germany (80.7).

locator.section: 4 Improving the health of the population

outcomes.statement: COVID-19 excess mortality was estimated at 102 per 100,000 people in 2020, 26% below the WHO European Region average, and fell to 42 in 2021 while the regional figure rose to 207.

locator.section: 4 Improving the health of the population

outcomes.statement: In the GBD 2019 study, Switzerland's Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index score for ages 0-74 was 92.6 (95% uncertainty interval 90.1-94.3) in 2019, 14.2 points higher than in 1990.

outcomes.statement: On the WHO UHC service coverage sub-indices for 2021, Switzerland scored highly on service capacity and access (97%), reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health (93%) and infectious diseases (92%), but lower on noncommunicable diseases (67%).

outcomes.statement: Infant mortality was 3.8 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2022, higher than in neighbouring countries and than in earlier years, when it ranged from 3.1 to 3.6.

locator.section: 4 Improving the health of the population

costs.statement: In 2021, health spending was US$8,998 per person (PPP), the second highest in the world after the United States (US$12,012) and nearly twice the EU average (US$4,733).
Health spending equalled 11.8% of GDP in 2021, a lower share than in Germany (12.9%), the UK (12.4%), France (12.3%) and Austria (12.1%) and well below the United States (17.4%).
Health costs were CHF 10,792 per person nationally in 2024, ranging from CHF 13,709 in Basel-Stadt to CHF 8,671 in Uri, 37% less.
Basic insurance (OKP) costs per insured person rose from CHF 1,723 in 1996 to CHF 4,482 in 2023.
Basic insurance costs rose 5.3% in 2025, again a strong increase compared with the average since the KVG came into force.
In 2021, long-term care took 20.6% of health spending, almost double the EU average (10.9%), while medical goods took 14.3%, below the EU average (19.4%).
Only 2.8% of current health spending went to preventive care in 2021, against an EU average of 5.1%.
A study cited by the European Observatory estimated the efficiency potential of services covered by mandatory insurance at 16-19% of its costs.

Using claims data from Switzerland's largest insurer, a 2026 study found that adults who chose a CHF 500 or a CHF 2,500 deductible had 11% and 27% lower health spending, respectively, than comparable adults with the CHF 300 minimum; the effects were larger for outpatient care and drugs.
Swiss health spending was 11.7% of GDP in 2022 in the OECD data used by Mirror, Mirror 2024, against 16.5% in the United States.

what_works.statement: Switzerland has consistently had the lowest premature mortality in Europe from the four major noncommunicable diseases (ages 30-69), at around 260 deaths per 100,000 in the early 2000s and falling since.

locator.section: 4 Improving the health of the population

what_works.statement: Few people report going without a medical examination because of cost: 0.8% in 2022, below the EU average of 1.1%, though 1.3% in the lowest income group against 0% in the highest.
In Mirror, Mirror 2024, Switzerland was among the three best performers on health outcomes (life expectancy, excess deaths in the pandemic and avoidable deaths), with Australia and New Zealand.
When Mirror, Mirror 2024 widened its equity measure to cover geography and gender, Switzerland ranked first, because of very small differences between rural and other areas and between men and women.

The federal health technology assessment programme, which removes ineffective services from basic insurance, now saves about CHF 150 million a year, according to a January 2026 Federal Council report.

The FOPH says that by reviewing covered services, regularly reviewing drug prices and checking tariff structures and contracts, the Department of Home Affairs and the FOPH saved more than CHF 2 billion in total over the past ten years.

problems.statement: The European Observatory finds that Switzerland's multilevel governance also causes inefficiency, fragmentation and slow progress on health reforms.

Coverage gaps remain for people between jobs or who do not know they are entitled to cantonal premium subsidies, which can cause temporary lapses; take-up of subsidies by eligible people is not monitored systematically in all cantons.

Because outpatient care is funded only from premiums, shifting care from inpatient to outpatient settings has steadily reduced the tax-funded share, and premiums have risen faster than total costs of KVG services, according to the FOPH.

In Geneva, a yearly population survey found the share of people forgoing health care for financial reasons rose from 15.8% in 2011 to 25.8% in 2025, while premiums rose 61.9%; across all years 18.1% reported forgoing care.

In 2024, 20% of Swiss adults aged 65 and over said they had forgone at least one health service because of cost (13% dental care, 13% services covered by basic insurance), compared with 21% in 2017 and 16% in 2021.
Unmet need for dental care was higher than for medical care, at 2.5% overall in 2021 and 4.6% in the poorest income fifth.
Primary care doctors are unevenly spread: urban areas have about 1 full-time-equivalent doctor per 1,000 inhabitants, rural areas 0.4.

locator.section: 3 Generating resources, providing services and ensuring access

problems.statement: In 2021, 38.4% of doctors working in Switzerland had trained abroad, one of the highest shares in the WHO European Region and up from 27.0% in 2012.
The share of doctors aged 55 or over rose from 32.9% in 2013 to 37.2% in 2021.
Mirror, Mirror 2024 suggests that the fragmentation of care delivery across Switzerland's many cantons and municipalities may be hampering efficiency for providers and patients.
In the sensitivity tests for Mirror, Mirror 2024, Switzerland was nearly always ranked near the bottom of the 10 countries overall.
Uptake of the electronic patient record has been slow, held back by interoperability problems, decentralized governance and resistance from providers and patients.
Tobacco use (age-standardized, ages 15 and over) was estimated at 22.8% in 2020, below the EU's 26.8%, but it has fallen only modestly from 27% in 2000.

locator.section: 4 Improving the health of the population

reforms.statement: After the indirect counter-proposal to the 2024 cost-brake initiative took effect, the Federal Council can set targets for cost and quality growth in basic insurance; it is due to set them for the first time at the end of 2026, for 2028-2031, and if costs in an area exceed the target, the Federal Council and cantons must consider corrective measures.

Since 1 January 2026, each canton must contribute a minimum amount to premium reductions, and within four years must set the maximum share of disposable income that premiums may take for its residents.

A canton's minimum contribution is 3.5% of the gross basic insurance costs of its residents if premiums take under 11% of the income of its lowest-income 40% of insured, rising linearly to 7.5% when they take 18.5% or more.
Voters rejected the 'premium relief' initiative, which would have capped premiums at 10% of income, on 9 June 2024, with 55.47% voting no; the counter-proposal on premium subsidies took its place.
On 24 November 2024, voters approved the KVG amendment for uniform financing of health services (EFAS) with 53.31% in favour.

From 2028 outpatient and inpatient care are to be financed the same way, and nursing care from 2032: the cantons will pay 26.9% of net costs (after patient cost-sharing) to insurers and premiums the remaining 73.1%.

Outpatient and primary care is paid fee-for-service under a national tariff schedule negotiated by insurers, provider associations and federal authorities; the TARDOC schedule is to replace TARMED from January 2026.

Cost-containment packages have been rolled out in stages: package 1a (2022-2023) brought billing transparency, outpatient flat-rate tariffs and a national tariff organization; cost targets for basic insurance were introduced in 2023; package 1b (2024) strengthened insurers' cost monitoring and widened pharmacists' ability to dispense cheaper drugs; and package 2, adopted in March 2025, extends federal oversight of reimbursement and promotes coordinated care.
According to a study published in January 2026, both chambers of parliament had recently voted to raise the minimum deductible from CHF 300 to CHF 500.
To ease regional shortages, Switzerland increased university places in human medicine from 900 in 2016 to a projected 1,350 by 2025.

us_lessons.statement: Mirror, Mirror 2024, which compares the US with nine other countries, names Switzerland together with Australia and New Zealand as worth studying for outcomes of care.
